unit_label: BFM Module C unit 5 (courseware unit 23): treasury risk management

facts.statement: Why treasury risk matters (courseware): treasury risk management matters because profits are generated from market opportunities and market risk is present at every step, and because treasury generates balance sheet risk for other departments. Concerns: (1) very high leverage: treasury can buy and sell foreign exchange of Rs 100 crore without any direct investment of funds (apart from capital allocated under capital adequacy), so a small adverse movement can cause a large loss of capital, whereas the loss on a loan is capped by the principal and interest and usually secured; (2) large transaction size at the sole discretion of the treasurer, with limits delegated in advance and little specific approval; (3) losses materialise in a very short time and confirmed transactions are irrevocable, so no corrective action is possible and open positions cannot be held long. The source of risk is variation in the market price of a currency or security (volatility); for a bond it is the interest rate (price and yield move inversely). Treasury also faces systematic risk (of the entire market) and unsystematic risk (of a particular investment) and funding or liquidity risk, since settlements must be funded; liquidity and interest rate risk are two sides of one coin; asset-liability management is closely connected to market risk.

Organisational controls (courseware): checks and balances in the system: the front office executes deals with counterparty banks (foreign exchange, securities, lending and borrowing) in the trading book, for clients (merchant book) or for the bank internal requirement; the back office confirms, accounts for and settles deals, obtaining independent confirmation from the counterparty and settling only if within the exposure limits for that counterparty, and verifies rates in deal slips against the market (screen rates noted at regular intervals), and has overall responsibility for compliance with exposure and position limits and accuracy of transaction detail; the mid-office is responsible for risk management and management information: monitoring compliance with the board-approved risk limits, regulatory compliance, daily mark-to-market valuation of positions, verification of pricing of treasury products, and periodic reports to top management, maintaining the overall risk profile and monitoring liquidity and interest rate risks in line with ALM guidelines. Front and back office must report independently to the Treasury Head and the Operations Head respectively; the mid-office may report to an executive outside Treasury such as the Chief Risk Officer.

Internal controls: position limits and stop-loss limits (courseware): limits on dealers trading in foreign exchange and securities are preventive measures against sudden market fluctuations. In foreign exchange there are three kinds: limits on deal size (the maximum value of a single buy or sell transaction, protecting against large losses on a deal; applies to trade deals, not merchant deals covered back to back), limits on open positions (unmatched buy and sell positions; carrying an open position has a carry cost such as the interest on funds used, and exposes the bank to exchange movements; limits are daylight (intra-day) and overnight, with overnight limits smaller because the market is active but untracked at night; limits are currency-wise and in aggregate in rupees, the currency-wise net positions being converted into USD at the day-end rate and then into rupees; overnight limits are pre-approved by the central bank) and stop-loss limits (the final control: when the market moves adversely, the open position is closed at a loss level acceptable to management; for example with a USD 5,000 stop loss, the dealer closes the position when the loss reaches that level). Stop-loss limits are prescribed per deal, per day, per month and as an aggregate loss limit; violations are viewed seriously; the back office monitors limits and valuation, informs the front office immediately of a breach; forex positions are marked to market daily. In swaps and forwards a matched deal can still lose if delivery dates differ; the risk in forward positions is measured by gaps (residual time) with gap limits per time bucket (aggregate gap limit capped at a multiple of capital); capital must be maintained against the net overnight open position (courseware: 9 per cent). For securities, limits cover size of securities held for trading and holding period, minimum credit rating for non-SLR securities, caps on maturity at portfolio level, duration and modified duration; stop-loss is applied through the mark-to-market value of the trading portfolio, with risk measures such as VaR and duration since securities markets are less liquid and price movements larger and more irregular.

Exposure ceiling limits (courseware): exposure limits protect against credit and counterparty risk. Credit risk in treasury has default risk (the borrowing bank fails to repay on the due date; in repo, price risk as well; inter-bank is relatively risk free but a weak bank can become bankrupt or face a run) and settlement risk (the counterparty fails to deliver or settle). Prudence requires not lending the whole surplus to a single bank, to avoid concentration. Settlement risk: ideally deals settle delivery versus payment (DvP); government securities settle against payment since both securities and funding accounts are with the central bank, and similar systems exist for corporate securities through depositories; in foreign exchange the settlement of two currency legs takes place in different time zones, so the risk of the counterparty failing to complete its leg arises; Payment versus Payment (PvP) through Continuous Linked Settlement (CLS) addresses this. Banks fix exposure limits for counterparties (banks, financial institutions, mutual funds, primary dealers, brokers) based on net worth, market reputation, track record and credit rating; limits take account of the size of treasury operations and vary with the period (overnight, 3 months, 6 months: the longer, the greater the risk, so the lower the limit); limits for brokers are fixed to avoid business concentration (courseware: a ceiling of 5 per cent of total business per year per broker); all limits are reviewed at least once a year; back office and mid-office ensure compliance.

Market risk and its components (courseware): a bank faces credit risk (loss of funds lent when the counterparty fails) and market risk (the value of an asset diminishes or the liability under an obligation increases because prices, interest rates or exchange rates move). Market risk is a confluence of liquidity risk, interest rate risk, exchange rate risk, equity risk and commodity risk; the Bank for International Settlements defines it as the risk that the value of on- or off-balance sheet positions will be adversely affected by movements in equity and interest rate markets, currency exchange rates and commodity prices. The three main components are liquidity risk, interest rate risk and currency risk. Liquidity risk is cash flow gaps that cannot be bridged (for example funds borrowed in the call market and invested in a five-year government security that cannot be sold when the market collapses, forcing borrowing at any cost); it is managed by knowing the due dates of money market placements and by a contingency plan for unforeseen events (invoked guarantees, premature deposit payment). Interest rate risk is the rise in interest costs of liabilities or fall in interest earnings from assets eroding profits; it arises wherever there is a mismatch between maturing assets and liabilities (for example one-year average deposits invested in three-month treasury bills whose yield is reset every three months and may fall below the deposit cost, making net earnings negative); a steep rise in rates can crash bond prices. Currency risk is a manifestation of interest rate risk; interest rate is the domestic cost of currency and the exchange rate the external cost; forward rates reflect interest rate differentials (distorted by supply and demand in the rupee case); exchange rates are influenced more by external trade, global interest rates and capital flows. Equity and commodity price risks matter even for treasuries with limited exposure because stock prices reflect overall liquidity and affect interest and exchange rates; banks in India are not permitted to take commodity exposures except for gold on account of customer requirement. Market risks are driven mainly by speculation, so the perception of future changes matters more than actual changes. Market risk translates into balance sheet risk, linked to ALM.

Value at Risk (courseware): VaR is a statistical measure of the worst possible movement of a market rate over a given period under normal market conditions at a defined confidence level. Example: an overnight VaR of 45 paise for USD/INR at 95 per cent confidence implies a 5 per cent chance that the rate will worsen by more than 45 paise next day; with the spot at Rs 75.00 the worst expected rate for exporters is Rs 74.55 (and for importers Rs 75.45) with 95 per cent confidence. For a yield: an overnight VaR of 0.35 per cent on a 7.75 per cent yield means a 95 per cent chance that the yield falls no lower than 7.40 per cent (buyer worst case) or rises no higher than 8.10 per cent (seller worst case) by next day. Methods: parametric (variance-covariance) based on volatility (the standard deviation of the rate over a period) multiplied by the number of standard deviations for the confidence level; Monte Carlo simulation of random scenarios; and historical simulation using actual past changes (for example the last 90 days), possibly giving progressive weight to recent data. VaR gives management a single absolute figure for potential loss; it measures currency, interest rate and price risks in a trading book, and is most commonly used for overnight or short horizons; for a longer period VaR is overnight VaR multiplied by the square root of the number of days (n), which is less accurate for long periods; back-testing is used to test the model.

Bond yield and price (courseware): a bond carries a coupon rate payable on par (face) value; traded price is above par (premium) or below par (discount) depending on market interest rates. Yield to maturity (YTM) is the discount rate at which the present value of all cash flows (interest and principal) equals the market price; at the YTM the net present value is zero; it assumes reinvestment of cash flows at the same rate. Current yield is the coupon divided by the price: the courseware example of a 5 per cent coupon bond with two years left bought at 98 has a current yield of 5.10 per cent. Price and yield move inversely: a rise in yield lowers the bond price. The YTM of two bonds may be the same but their price risk (sensitivity) may differ because of maturity or frequency of coupons, so YTM is not comparable as a measure of price volatility.

Duration and modified duration (courseware): duration (Macaulay duration) is the weighted average life of a bond, with each cash flow weighted by the time of receipt multiplied by its present value, divided by the market price (the sum of present values); it is expressed in years. The longer the duration, the greater the sensitivity of price to interest rate changes; it allows comparison of bonds of different structures. The duration of a zero coupon bond equals its time to maturity. For a bond portfolio, the weighted average duration is found by weighting each bond duration by its market value share; a treasurer can immunise a portfolio against interest rate risk by keeping the average duration equal to a target holding period. Modified duration (MD) = Macaulay duration / (1 + yield); the percentage change in price for a given yield change is approximately -MD x change in yield. Example: duration 2.5, yield 5 per cent gives MD = 2.5 / 1.05 = 2.38, and a rise of 5 basis points lowers the price by about 2.38 x 0.05 = 0.12 per cent (12 basis points). Limits: valid for small changes; exact price change differs because the yield curve is not a straight line, so a convexity adjustment is made (modified duration is the first order, convexity the second order effect). Duration applies to bank assets (loans) and liabilities (borrowings); the difference between the duration of assets and liabilities is the duration gap, used for macro hedging of balance sheet risk.

Derivatives for risk management (courseware): derivatives are contracts that derive value from an underlying market for a commodity or financial product; they protect treasury transactions from market risk and manage balance sheet (asset-liability) risk. For example, if an asset is very sensitive to interest rate changes and rates are expected to rise, the bank can swap fixed rate interest for floating rate with an interest rate swap; exchange rate risk can be avoided by a forward contract or option. The summary points: market risk consists of liquidity and interest rate risk (two sides of a coin), with exchange rate, equity and commodity price risk identified separately; conventional controls include checking accuracy of deals through confirmation, compliance with risk limits, exposure limits for counterparties and intra-day and overnight limits on open positions and stop-loss limits; limits on open positions need prior approval of the central bank; VaR is the maximum loss in a time horizon at a given confidence level under normal circumstances; duration measures interest rate sensitivity.

payload.title: Why treasury risk needs special management
payload.core_explanation_md:
Treasury risk matters because **profit comes from market opportunities** (so **market risk is present at every step**) and because treasury creates **balance sheet risk** for other departments.

**Three concerns:**

1. **High leverage:** a dealer can trade **Rs 100 crore of currency** with almost **no funds invested**, so a **small adverse move** can wipe out a lot of capital. A **loan loss is capped** at principal and interest and usually **secured**.
2. **Large deals at the sole discretion of the treasurer**, with limits **delegated in advance**.
3. **Losses arrive fast** and **confirmed deals are irrevocable**; open positions **cannot be held long**.

**Source of risk:** the **market price** of a currency or security (**volatility**). **Systematic risk** is market-wide; **unsystematic risk** is specific to one investment. Treasury also faces **funding (liquidity) risk**, since settlements must be funded.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Leverage turns small price moves into large losses against capital.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is treasury risk greater than loan risk for the same capital?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Treasury is highly leveraged, so a small price move can cause a loss far larger than the capital behind it, while a loan loss is capped at the amount lent.

payload.title: Organisational controls: front, back and mid-office
payload.core_explanation_md:
| Office | Role in control |
| --- | --- |
| **Front office** | **Executes deals** (trading book, merchant book, internal needs) |
| **Back office** | **Confirms** each deal **independently with the counterparty**, **settles only within exposure limits**, **checks rates** against screen rates, ensures **compliance with limits** and **accuracy of detail** |
| **Mid-office** | **Risk management and MIS**: monitors **board-approved limits**, **regulatory compliance**, **daily mark-to-market**, **verifies pricing**, **reports to top management**, watches **liquidity and interest rate risk** in line with ALM |

Front and back office **report independently** (to the **Treasury Head** and **Operations Head**). The mid-office may report to an executive **outside Treasury**, such as the **Chief Risk Officer**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Independent confirmation exposes a dealer who books a deal at a wrong or hidden price.

self_check.prompt_text: Who confirms each deal with the counterparty?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The back office, independently of the dealer.

payload.title: Position limits and stop-loss limits
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Three kinds of forex trading limits:**

| Limit | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Deal size** | **Maximum value of one buy or sell**; protects against a large loss on a deal; applies to **trade deals** (not back-to-back merchant deals) |
| **Open position** | Limit on **unmatched** positions; carries a **cost of carry** (interest on funds used) and **exchange risk**; **daylight (intra-day)** and **overnight** limits, with **overnight smaller** because the market runs unobserved; **currency-wise** and **aggregate in rupees** (net positions converted to USD at the day-end rate, then to rupees); **overnight limits pre-approved by the central bank** |
| **Stop-loss** | The **final control**: the position is **closed when the loss reaches** a set level; set **per deal, per day, per month** and as an **aggregate** |

**Forwards and swaps:** even matched deals can lose if **delivery dates differ**; the risk is measured by **gaps** (residual time) with **gap limits** per time bucket and an **aggregate gap limit** capped at a multiple of capital. **Capital** must be held against the **net overnight open position**.

**Securities:** limits on **size held for trading**, **holding period**, **minimum credit rating** (non-SLR), **maturity**, **duration and modified duration**; stop-loss via **mark-to-market of the trading portfolio** and **VaR**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A stop-loss stops a dealer hoping that a losing position will recover.

self_check.prompt_text: Why are overnight open position limits smaller than daylight limits?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The market stays active overnight but positions are not tracked, so the risk is higher.

payload.title: Exposure ceilings: default risk and settlement risk
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Exposure limits** protect against **credit and counterparty risk**.

- **Default risk:** the borrowing bank **fails to repay** on the due date (in a repo there is also **price risk**). Even inter-bank is not risk-free; a weak bank can fail or face a run. **Do not lend the whole surplus to one bank**: avoid **concentration**.
- **Settlement risk:** the counterparty **fails to deliver or settle**. **DvP** removes it for securities (government securities settle against payment since both accounts are with the central bank). In **forex**, the two currency legs settle in **different time zones**, leaving **settlement risk**; **PvP through Continuous Linked Settlement (CLS)** addresses it.

**Setting limits:** by counterparty **net worth, reputation, track record and rating**; sized to the **scale of treasury operations**; **tighter for longer periods** (overnight, 3 months, 6 months); **limits on brokers** to avoid business concentration; **reviewed at least yearly**; compliance ensured by **back and mid-office**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The longer an exposure lasts, the more can go wrong, so its limit is lower.

self_check.prompt_text: What does PvP through CLS address?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The settlement risk that arises when the two legs of a foreign exchange deal settle in different time zones.

payload.title: Market risk and its components
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Credit risk** is loss from a counterparty failing. **Market risk** is loss because **prices, interest rates or exchange rates** move so that an asset loses value or a liability rises. The **BIS** definition: the risk that **on- or off-balance sheet positions** lose value because of movements in **equity markets, interest rates, exchange rates and commodity prices**.

**Components:**

| Risk | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Liquidity risk** | **Cash flow gaps** cannot be bridged (for example call money funding a five-year bond that cannot be sold); managed by **knowing due dates** and a **contingency plan** |
| **Interest rate risk** | Rising **funding costs** or falling **asset earnings**; arises from **mismatch** of maturing assets and liabilities |
| **Currency risk** | **Exchange rate moves**; it is one face of interest rate risk, since the **interest rate is what a currency costs at home and the exchange rate what it costs abroad** |

**Equity and commodity risks** matter even for limited exposures because they affect **liquidity, interest and exchange rates**. Banks in India may not take commodity exposures except **gold for customers**. Markets are driven by **speculation**, so **perceived future change** matters more than actual change.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Liquidity and interest rate risk are two sides of one coin.

self_check.prompt_text: What are the three main components of market risk?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Liquidity risk, interest rate risk and currency risk.

payload.title: Value at Risk (VaR)
payload.core_explanation_md:
**VaR** is the **worst movement expected over a period, at a stated confidence level, under normal market conditions**.

Example: **overnight VaR of 45 paise** at **95 per cent** on USD/INR at **75.00**: there is only a **5 per cent chance** the rate worsens by more than 45 paise next day, so the worst rate is **74.55 for an exporter** and **75.45 for an importer**.

**Methods:**

1. **Parametric (variance-covariance)**: **volatility** (standard deviation) x **number of standard deviations** for the confidence level.
2. **Monte Carlo simulation**: random scenarios.
3. **Historical simulation**: actual past changes (for example 90 days), possibly **weighting recent data more**.

VaR gives **one absolute figure** for potential loss in currency, interest rate and price risk. For a longer horizon: **VaR(n days) = overnight VaR x square root of n** (less accurate for long periods). **Back-testing** checks the model.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: VaR says how bad a normal bad day can be, not how bad the worst day can be.

self_check.prompt_text: How is overnight VaR scaled to a ten-day horizon?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It is multiplied by the square root of ten.

payload.title: Parametric VaR and horizon scaling
payload.core_explanation_md:
**VaR = z x sigma x position value**, where **sigma** is the daily volatility and **z** the number of standard deviations (about **1.645** for **95 per cent** one-sided, **2.326** for **99 per cent**).

**n-day VaR = 1-day VaR x sqrt(n).**

**Worst-case rate for a long position (exporter selling USD) = spot - VaR**; for a short position = spot + VaR.

Example: daily volatility **0.30 per cent** on **Rs 50 crore**, 95 per cent: VaR = **1.645 x 0.003 x 50 = Rs 0.247 crore**; for **9 days**: **x 3 = Rs 0.740 crore**.

variables.name: Standard deviations for the confidence level

common_errors: Scaling by n instead of the square root of n
Using the two-sided z for a one-sided worst case

payload.expanded_explanation_md: Square-root scaling assumes changes on different days are independent.

self_check.prompt_text: Which z is used for a one-sided 95 per cent VaR?

payload.title: Bond price, yield and current yield
payload.core_explanation_md:
A bond pays a **coupon on par value**; it trades at a **premium or discount** to par depending on market interest rates.

- **Yield to maturity (YTM):** the single discount rate that makes the **present value of all the bond's cash flows equal to its market price** (NPV at YTM is zero); it assumes **reinvestment at the same rate**.
- **Current yield = coupon / price.** Example: 5 per cent coupon, price 98: **5.10 per cent**.
- **Price and yield move inversely**.
- Two bonds with the same YTM can have **different price sensitivity** (maturity, coupon frequency), so YTM is **not a measure of price volatility**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Bought at a discount, YTM exceeds current yield, which exceeds the coupon rate.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the current yield of a 6 per cent coupon bond priced at 96?

payload.title: Macaulay duration, modified duration and price change
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Macaulay duration D = sum of t x PV(cash flow t) / price**, in **years**.

**Modified duration MD = D / (1 + y).**

**Percentage price change = - MD x change in yield** (approximately, for small changes).

**Zero coupon bond:** D equals **time to maturity**.

**Portfolio duration** = **market-value weighted** average of bond durations.

**Duration gap = duration of assets - duration of liabilities** (as the courseware states it), used for balance sheet interest rate risk.

Example: **D = 2.5, y = 5 per cent**: MD = **2.38**; yield **+5 bp** gives about **-0.12 per cent** price (**12 bp**).

common_errors: Using duration instead of modified duration for price change

payload.expanded_explanation_md: Longer duration means a larger price fall for a given yield rise.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the duration of a zero coupon bond?

payload.title: Limits of duration, convexity and duration gap
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Duration** is valid for **small changes** in yield and is **not uniform** at different yield levels: price change is proportional to the yield change **only if the yield curve is a straight line**. In practice the term structure is not, so an **adjustment for convexity** is made. **Modified duration** is the **first-order** effect and **convexity** the **second-order** effect.

**A treasurer can immunise** a bond portfolio by holding **average duration equal to the target holding period** (rebalancing as time passes).

In the balance sheet, the **duration of assets (loans)** and **liabilities (borrowings)** show how sensitive earnings are to rates; their **difference is the duration gap**, used for **macro-hedging**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Convexity corrects duration for the curvature of the price-yield relation.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is a convexity adjustment needed?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Because the price-yield relation is curved, so duration alone is accurate only for small yield changes.

payload.title: Using derivatives to manage risk
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Derivatives** derive value from an underlying commodity or financial market. They **protect treasury transactions** from market risk and help **manage balance sheet (ALM) risk**.

- If an **asset is very sensitive to interest rates** and rates are expected to **rise**, the bank can **swap fixed rate for floating rate** (an **interest rate swap**).
- **Exchange rate risk** can be avoided with a **forward contract or an option**.

**Summary of controls:** deal **confirmation**, **compliance with limits**, **counterparty exposure limits**, **intra-day and overnight open position limits** (prior central bank approval) and **stop-loss limits**. **VaR** is the **maximum loss over a horizon at a confidence level in normal conditions**; **duration** measures **interest rate sensitivity**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A derivative lets the bank change the risk without selling the underlying asset.

self_check.prompt_text: How can a bank protect an interest-sensitive asset if it expects rates to rise?
self_check.expected_takeaway: By entering an interest rate swap to pay fixed and receive floating (swap fixed rate for floating).

unresolved: The unit is conceptual treasury risk management with no regulator-specific figures except: the 6 times capital aggregate gap limit, the 9 per cent capital charge on the net overnight open position limit (NOOPL) or outstanding position, the 5 per cent cap on business with an individual broker, and overnight position limits pre-approved by the central bank. These are stated by the courseware as at its date, were not checked against primary sources and are not taught or tested as current rules; items that need a percentage state it as an assumption.

The courseware worked bond example (5 per cent coupon, price 98, two years left, YTM stated as 6.08 per cent, current yield 5.10 per cent) was recomputed: with annual coupons the YTM is 6.09 per cent (6.0923); the courseware figure differs in the second decimal, probably by rounding or a different compounding convention. The courseware duration example (duration 2.5 years, yield 5 per cent, modified duration 2.38, a 5 basis point rise lowering the price by about 12 basis points) was recomputed and agrees. Items use annual coupons and new figures, computed in the test.

The courseware VaR example (a 45 paise overnight VaR at 95 per cent on USD/INR at 75.00 giving 75.45 or 74.55; a 0.35 per cent yield VaR on a 7.75 per cent yield) was recomputed and agrees. The statement that VaR is additive across asset classes is a courseware statement; in general VaR is not additive unless risks are perfectly correlated, so it is not taught as a rule. The statement that a 95 per cent VaR "implies a 5 per cent chance of the rate worsening beyond" is taught as the courseware interpretation (one-sided).
The courseware treats the square-root-of-time scaling of overnight VaR as the method for longer horizons and notes that it is not accurate for long periods; taught as stated.

The courseware states the duration of a zero coupon bond equals the time to maturity, and that Macaulay duration and modified duration relate as D divided by one plus yield; both are taught. The courseware describes convexity only briefly and it is not computed.
The courseware describes credit risk, liquidity risk, systematic and unsystematic risk and market risk in prose; the BIS definition of market risk is taught as stated.
Numbers in the numerical items are invented and checked in tests/content/batch-bfm-c-u05-b001.test.ts, including duration, modified duration, price change, VaR and scaling.
